mcqs.question: Why does a feed ranking system use a multi-stage funnel instead of running one rich ranking model over every candidate post?
options: Because a rich, expensive ranking model can't afford to run over millions of posts under a tight latency budget, so a cheap candidate-generation stage narrows the pool first
Because ranking models cannot be trained on more than a few hundred examples
Because candidate generation always produces more accurate scores than the ranking stage
Because business rules must always run before any ML model touches the data
mcqs.explanation: The funnel exists purely to keep the expensive ranking model's workload small enough for the latency budget — candidate generation trades some precision for speed specifically so the ranker doesn't have to run at full catalog scale. Training set size isn't the constraint, candidate generation is intentionally less accurate (not more) than ranking, and business rules run last, not first.

mcqs.question: What is the underlying reason optimizing purely for engagement breeds outrage-bait and addictive content in a feed?
options: Engagement-based models are only trained on video content, which is inherently more provocative
The ranking model has no notion of 'valuable to the user' beyond whatever proxy signal it was trained to maximize, so it amplifies anything that drives that proxy regardless of actual value
The candidate generation stage filters out all non-controversial content before ranking even begins
Outrage-bait only happens when the feed uses collaborative filtering instead of content-based filtering
mcqs.explanation: The core issue is a proxy-objective mismatch: the model faithfully maximizes whatever engagement signal it's given, and that signal doesn't distinguish 'valuable' from 'provocative.' It's not specific to video, candidate generation doesn't filter for controversy, and the effect isn't tied to any one specific recommendation algorithm family.

mcqs.question: Why does candidate generation typically use a two-tower model while the ranking stage uses a model that can process cross-features directly?
options: Two-tower embeddings let content-side vectors be precomputed offline and searched via fast nearest-neighbor lookup, which cross-feature models can't do since their score depends on the specific user-content pair at query time
Two-tower models are always more accurate than cross-feature models, so ranking would use them too if it could
Cross-feature models cannot run in production at any scale
Two-tower models require no training data, unlike ranking models
mcqs.explanation: The two-tower shape is chosen for retrieval speed: because the two sides are scored independently, content embeddings can be precomputed and indexed for fast ANN search, which a model needing user-content cross-features at scoring time cannot support cheaply. It's not about which model family is more accurate in general, ranking models do run in production (just on a much smaller candidate set), and both need training data.

mcqs.question: A feed ranking model shows improved offline normalized cross-entropy against held-out engagement labels. What's the correct next step before shipping it?
options: Ship it immediately, since improved offline metrics on held-out data are sufficient proof of a better user experience
Retrain the offline model on the same data repeatedly until the metric stops improving, then ship
Skip the A/B test and only check whether engineering complexity increased
Run a live A/B test gated on session and longer-horizon metrics like retention, since offline metrics only measure fit to the proxy labels, not the true user-value objective
mcqs.explanation: An offline metric win is only a candidate for shipping — it reflects fit to proxy labels, not the actual objective, so a live A/B test tracking real session and retention metrics is needed to confirm it's genuinely better, not just better at predicting the proxy. Shipping on offline metrics alone, or ignoring user-facing validation, risks exactly the engagement-optimization trap covered elsewhere in this topic.
